title: Make Sure They Have Their Time
author: The Daily Dad
summary: This short Daily Dad reflection argues that busy parents must deliberately schedule protected time with their children, or the children will be the first thing squeezed out. It acknowledges the competing claims of work, marriage and adult obligations, then observes that when parents wing it, kids absorb the cost because they are easiest to put off with a screen, an errand or a quick "I'm busy right now." The piece's main illustration is Ruth Bader Ginsburg's routine in law school: studying between classes while a nanny was present, then treating four o'clock onward as her daughter Jane's time before returning to her books after bedtime. The central move is to reframe time with children as non-negotiable in the same way as work commitments, and to challenge parents who justify long hours as being for their family. If children are truly the priority, the essay concludes, they should receive not leftovers but the best time.
points: The essay warns that unstructured days predictably sacrifice children first, since they are the easiest to postpone with TV, errands or deferral.
Ruth Bader Ginsburg's fixed daily handoff at four o'clock is offered as a model of rigid scheduling that protected time with her daughter under intense pressure.
Time with children should be treated as non-negotiable, on par with work obligations, rather than whatever remains at the end of the day.
Fathers who claim to work hard for their families are challenged to prove it by giving children their best hours, not their leftovers.
quotes: The truth is, if you’re winging it everyday, you won’t get it all in. Something will fall by the wayside and too often, that’s our kids.
Because we can turn on the TV. Because we can strap them in the car seat and bring them along on errands. Because we can tell them, “Sorry, kiddo. I’m busy right now.
This is why it can be a good idea to have very specific, scheduled time.

I used the time in between classes to study, to read the next day’s assignment, but 4 o’clock was Jane’s time. We went to the park, played games, sang silly songs. When she went to sleep, I went back to the books.
You gotta make sure they have their time. Non-negotiable time, just as you do with work or anything else. The kids don’t get your leftovers.
What does it say if that’s all we give them? No, they are the priority. Especially if we go around claiming that we are working so hard for our family.
